figures.caption: Figure 4: Additional Case Study. Given an image of Lons-le-Saunier, the goal is to fetch the missing table evidence (the list of principal cities of Franche-Comte) to complete the evidence set.

Table 9: Sequencial Pool Construction performance comparison between GRAIL (ours) and without Wmix on the MultimodalQA dataset. Improvements in SetRecall@10 and Noise-Resilience Margin (NRM) are relative to the Query Only model (44.69% Set-Rec@10). Rank Jump values and their standard deviations are formatted as mean (std.dev.).

Figure 1: Redundancy trap in MMQA. Given a table and three emblems, the goal is to fetch the missing visual evidence (Bolton Wanderers’s emblem) to complete the evidence set. (i) Query + Context fail as they trapped by the existing Lancashire Senior Cup context (Semantic Anchoring). Meanwhile, Explicit Rewriting (IRCoT) prematurely concludes the search upon verifying Manchester City’s record, overlooking the unexamined visual assets. (ii) Query − Context succeeds by implicitly subtracting the covered context features within the embedding space, shifting the search direction toward the unobserved visual target. See Appendix A for another case study.

Table 2: Implicit vs. Explicit query modeling performance and latency. We evaluated macro-averaged recall across the MultimodalQA validation split (2,724 data, q_type ∈{Compare, Compose, Intersect}). Our GRAIL & Hybrid consistently outperform both the additive baseline and explicit query regeneration baselines.

Figure 2: Hybrid framework leveraging complementary specialists in MultimodalQA. By dynamically routing each query to the optimal specialist, our hybrid framework achieves a "best-of-both-worlds" performance (+40.3% macro avg. gain over Additive).

Figure 8: Breakdown of additional retrieval gains by question type. The bars represent the isolated increase in Set-Recall contributed exclusively by the 7 additional evidence pieces retrieved after the initial Query Only baseline (Base 3). Note that the baseline recall at Base 3 is omitted, plotting only the net incremental gain captured during the remaining sequential rescue steps (partitioning scheme 3+2+3+2). All values represent the percentage point (%pp) improvement, mapping the distinct behavior of the static Query Only baseline, the Additive model, and our Gap-Aware mechanism across the four question categories of MultimodalQA dataset.

Figure 7: Set Recall across varying pool sizes (K). The leftmost dashed segment represents the initial Base (Query Only) retrieval, while subsequent segments illustrate cumulative gains from the sequential execution of iterative GRAIL slices (e.g., [3+2]*2 denotes a 3(base)+2+3+2 step sequence, darkening chronologically). Across all pool sizes, our iterative framework consistently expands retrieval coverage, demonstrating sustained gains even as the retrieval constraints scale.

Table 16: Inference efficiency and operational cost comparison. All configurations utilize precomputed asset embeddings, requiring zero evidence encoder passes during inference. GRAIL completely eliminates the autoregressive LLM inference loop required by explicit query generation baselines, achieving millisecond-level latency and zero API cost while maintaining robustness to retrieval noise.

Figure 6: Model specialization by task complexity in MultimodalQA. Additive models excel in Uni-modal lookup, while Gap-aware models dominate reasoningheavy tasks (Compare, Compose). This performance gap remains consistent across alignment architectures.

Table 3: Granular efficiency under various step configurations (K = 10). Performance changes are relative to the Query Only baseline; Jump values are reported as mean (90th percentile). Results demonstrate that sequential GRAIL outperforms both static additive interpolation and single-shot retrieval, effectively compensating for the scarcity of initial context.

Table 15: Granular efficiency under various step configurations (K = 10) in WebQA. Relative improvements are measured related to Query Only baseline. GRAIL maintains robust, positive margins across granular partition schedules, whereas the Additive framework suffers severe performance degradation.
Table 14: Retrieval performance across question types in WebQA. Comparison between the Additive baseline and GRAIL subject to q_type.

Figure 5: Taxonomy of cross-modal semantic alignment. Top row shows query-independent approaches: (a) Centroid-based alignment, (b) CLS-based alignment. Bottom row shows query-dependent approaches: (c) Query-evidence alignment, (d) Query-set alignment.
